title: "Leaflet Municipios"
output: html_document
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = TRUE,
  fig.dim = c(6, 6),
  dpi = 100,
  out.width = "100%"
)
```

This document provides examples of how to create interactive choropleth maps of Mexican municipios using the `mxmaps` and `leaflet` packages. The examples show how to visualize data for all municipios, as well as how to create focused maps of specific areas, such as cities or metropolitan areas, by subsetting the data.

```{r message=FALSE}
library("mxmaps")
library("sf")
library("leaflet") # for colorNumeric

df_mxmunicipio_2025$value <- df_mxmunicipio_2025$indigenous /
  df_mxmunicipio_2025$pop
# Viridis color scheme
magma <- c(
  "#000004FF", "#1D1146FF", "#50127CFF", "#822681FF", "#B63779FF",
  "#E65163FF", "#FB8761FF", "#FEC387FF", "#FCFDBFFF"
)
pal <- colorNumeric(magma, domain = df_mxmunicipio_2025$value)
mxmunicipio_leaflet(
  df = df_mxmunicipio_2025,
  pal = pal,
  fillColor = ~ pal(value),
  fillOpacity = .7,
  weight = .8,
  popup = ~ sprintf(
    "State: %s<br/>Municipio : %s<br/>Percent Indigenous: %s%%",
    state_name, municipio_name, round(value * 100, 1)
  )
) |>
  addLegend(
    position = "bottomright",
    pal = pal,
    values = df_mxmunicipio_2025$value,
    title = "Percent<br>Indigenous",
    labFormat = labelFormat(
      suffix = "%",
      transform = function(x) {
        100 * x
      }
    )
  ) |>
  addProviderTiles("Esri.WorldShadedRelief")
```

## City maps

You can also subset the data to only show certain municipios

```{r message=FALSE,warning=FALSE}
library("dplyr")
library("geojsonio")
library("jsonlite")
library("RColorBrewer")

df <- df_mxmunicipio_2020 |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  filter(metro_area %in% c("Valle de México", "Toluca", "Puebla-Tlaxcala"))

df$value <- df$indigenous / df$pop

Reds <- c("white", brewer.pal(4, "RdYlBu"))
pal <- colorNumeric(Reds, domain = df$value)
mxmunicipio_leaflet(
  df = df,
  fillColor = ~ pal(value),
  fillOpacity = 0.5,
  zoom = df$region,
  popup = sprintf(
    "State: %s<br/>Municipio : %s<br/>Value: %s%%",
    df$state_name,
    df$municipio_name,
    round(df$value * 100, 1)
  )
) |>
  addLegend(
    position = "bottomright",
    pal = pal,
    values = df$value
  )  |>
  addProviderTiles("Esri.WorldTerrain")
```


or you can subset the topoJSON directly

```{r message=FALSE,warning=FALSE}
# Convert the topoJSON to spatial object
tmpdir <- tempdir()

# Convert sf to GeoJSON string
geojson_str <- geojsonio::geojson_json(mxmunicipio.topoJSON)

# Convert GeoJSON to TopoJSON
topojson_str <- geojsonio::geo2topo(as.character(geojson_str))

# Write to a file
writeLines(topojson_str, file.path(tmpdir, "mun.topojson"))

muns <- topojson_read(file.path(tmpdir, "mun.topojson"))

# municipios that make up Monterrey
monterrey <- muns[
  muns$id %in%
    df_mxmunicipio_2020$region[
      df_mxmunicipio_2020$metro_area == "Monterrey"
    ],
]
# Convert to SpatialDataFrame
monterrey <- as_Spatial(monterrey)
# made-up data
monterrey@data$rand <- seq_len(nrow(monterrey@data))

# Create a continuous palette function
pal <- colorNumeric(
  palette = "Blues",
  domain = monterrey@data$rand
)

leaflet(monterrey) |>
  addPolygons(
    stroke = TRUE,
    smoothFactor = 0.2,
    fillOpacity = .7,
    weight = 1.2,
    fillColor = ~ pal(monterrey@data$rand),
    color = "#111"
  )  |>
  addProviderTiles("Esri.WorldTerrain")
```
